preliminaries.publisher_note: Rule of the Road is the popular name for the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea, 1972 (COLREGs, ROR). The Convention has 41 rules in six Parts (A to F): General; Steering and Sailing; Lights and Shapes; Sound and Light Signals; Exemptions; Verification of Compliance.
principles: Rule 2 ('rule of good seamanship') allows departure from the letter of the Rules to avoid immediate danger; strict literal compliance is no defence if a collision occurs.
The Rules mainly allocate which vessel keeps out of the way (give-way) and which maintains course and speed (stand-on).
Use of VHF to agree manoeuvres instead of following the Rules is discouraged.
Statistics quoted in the publisher's note: about 74 per cent of reported incidents relate to uncertainty, violations and disregard of the Rules.

rules.title: Application
rules.summary: The Rules apply to all vessels on the high seas and in connected waters navigable by seagoing vessels.

paragraphs.summary: Applies to all vessels on the high seas and connected navigable waters.
Local authorities may make special rules for roadsteads, harbours, rivers, lakes and inland waterways connected to the sea; these must conform as closely as possible to the Rules.
States may make extra rules on station/signal lights, shapes or whistle signals for warships, vessels sailing under convoy and fishing fleets; they must not be mistakable for any signal in the Rules.
IMO may adopt traffic separation schemes (see Rule 10).
A vessel of special construction or purpose that cannot fully comply with the light, shape or sound-signal provisions must comply as closely as her Government decides is possible.

rules.title: Responsibility
rules.summary: Nothing in the Rules excuses a vessel, owner, master or crew from the consequences of neglecting the Rules or any precaution required by ordinary seamanship or the special circumstances. The Rules may be departed from to avoid immediate danger. Known as the rule of good seamanship.

paragraphs.summary: No exoneration for neglect of the Rules or of precautions required by ordinary practice of seamen or special circumstances.

In construing and complying, due regard must be had to all dangers of navigation and collision and to special circumstances, including limitations of the vessels involved, which may make a departure from the Rules necessary to avoid immediate danger.

simulator_hooks: Collision always counts against own ship's record regardless of who was give-way (no vessel is excused).

rules.title: General definitions
rules.summary: Defines the terms used in the Rules (vessel, power-driven vessel, sailing vessel, fishing, seaplane, NUC, RAM, CBD, underway, length/breadth, in sight, restricted visibility, WIG craft).

paragraphs.summary: Every kind of watercraft, including non-displacement craft, WIG craft and seaplanes, used or capable of being used for transport on water.
Any vessel propelled by machinery.
Any vessel under sail provided propelling machinery, if fitted, is not being used. Using the engine makes her a power-driven vessel.
A vessel fishing with nets, lines, trawls or other apparatus that restricts manoeuvrability; trolling lines or gear that does not restrict manoeuvrability does not count.
Any aircraft designed to manoeuvre on the water.
A vessel that, through some exceptional circumstance, cannot manoeuvre as the Rules require and so cannot keep out of the way of another vessel.

paragraphs.term: vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (RAM)
paragraphs.summary: A vessel restricted by the nature of her work from manoeuvring as the Rules require. Includes (not limited to): laying/servicing/picking up a navigation mark, cable or pipeline; dredging, surveying or underwater operations; replenishment or transfer of persons/provisions/cargo underway; launching or recovering aircraft; mine clearance; towing that severely restricts the tug and tow from deviating.
examples: navigation mark, submarine cable or pipeline work

paragraphs.summary: A power-driven vessel that, because of her draught relative to the available depth and width of navigable water, is severely restricted in her ability to deviate from her course.
Not at anchor, made fast to the shore, or aground. A vessel can be underway and stopped (not making way).
Length overall and greatest breadth.
Only when one can be observed visually from the other (binoculars count, radar alone does not).
Any condition where visibility is restricted by fog, mist, falling snow, heavy rainstorms, sandstorms or similar causes.
A multi-modal craft that in its main operating mode flies in close proximity to the surface using surface-effect action.

rules.title: Application (Section I)
rules.summary: Section I rules (Rules 4 to 10) apply in any condition of visibility.

rules.title: Look-out
rules.summary: Every vessel must at all times keep a proper look-out by sight and hearing and by all available means suited to the circumstances, to make a full appraisal of the situation and of the risk of collision.

paragraphs.summary: Proper look-out by sight, hearing and all available means (radar, AIS, VHF etc.) at all times.

simulator_hooks: A look-out lapse can be modelled as detection delay / late risk assessment.

rules.title: Safe speed
rules.summary: Every vessel must proceed at a safe speed so she can take proper and effective action to avoid collision and be stopped within a distance appropriate to the circumstances.

paragraphs.summary: All vessels weigh: state of visibility; traffic density (incl. fishing vessels); manoeuvrability, especially stopping distance and turning ability; at night, background light such as shore lights or backscatter from own lights; state of wind, sea, current and nearby hazards; draught in relation to available depth.
factors: manoeuvrability / stopping distance and turning ability

paragraphs.summary: Vessels with operational radar must also weigh: characteristics, efficiency and limitations of the radar; constraints of the range scale in use; effect of sea state, weather and interference; small vessels, ice and floating objects may not be detected early; number, location and movement of vessels detected; more exact visibility assessment possible using radar range.
factors: small vessels and ice may be missed
number and movement of detected vessels

simulator_hooks: Own speed above safe speed in restricted visibility should raise a warning (R6, R19(b)).

rules.title: Risk of collision
rules.summary: Every vessel must use all available means to decide whether risk of collision exists. If in doubt, risk is deemed to exist.

paragraphs.summary: Use all available means; if there is any doubt, risk shall be deemed to exist.
Make proper use of radar if fitted and working, including long-range scanning for early warning, and radar plotting or equivalent systematic observation of detected objects.
Do not base assumptions on scanty information, especially scanty radar information.

Risk is deemed to exist if the compass bearing of an approaching vessel does not appreciably change. Risk may sometimes exist even with appreciable bearing change, particularly when approaching a very large vessel or a tow, or when at close range.
paragraphs.test: constant bearing with decreasing range = risk of collision

simulator_hooks: Risk flag: closing range with CPA below the CPA limit, or a steady bearing.

rules.title: Action to avoid collision
rules.summary: Action to avoid collision must follow the Rules and, if circumstances allow, be positive, made in ample time and with good seamanship. Alterations must be large enough to be readily apparent to another vessel observing visually or by radar.

paragraphs.summary: Action shall be in accordance with the Rules and, if circumstances admit, positive, in ample time and with due regard to good seamanship.
Alterations of course and/or speed shall be large enough to be readily apparent visually or by radar; avoid a succession of small alterations.

With sufficient sea room, an alteration of course alone may be the most effective action to avoid a close-quarters situation, if made in good time, substantial and not creating another close-quarters situation.
Action taken to avoid collision shall result in passing at a safe distance. Its effectiveness must be checked carefully until the other vessel is finally past and clear.
If necessary to avoid collision or allow more time to assess, a vessel shall slacken speed or take all way off by stopping or reversing means.

(i) A vessel required not to impede the passage or safe passage of another shall take early action to allow sufficient sea room. (ii) That vessel is not relieved of the obligation if risk of collision exists, and shall act as the Rules of Part B Sections II and III require when the vessels approach each other. (iii) A vessel whose passage is not to be impeded remains fully obliged to comply when the vessels approach so that collision is possible.

simulator_hooks: Early = before TCPA alarm; substantial = course change >= apparentDeg or speed change >= about 1 kn; check CPA after the action.

rules.title: Narrow channels
rules.summary: Keep as near to the outer limit of the channel on your starboard side as is safe and practicable.

paragraphs.summary: A vessel proceeding along a narrow channel or fairway shall keep as near to the outer limit of the channel or fairway on her starboard side as is safe and practicable.
A vessel of less than 20 m or a sailing vessel shall not impede the passage of a vessel that can safely navigate only within a narrow channel or fairway.
A vessel engaged in fishing shall not impede the passage of any other vessel navigating within a narrow channel or fairway.

A vessel shall not cross a narrow channel or fairway if crossing impedes a vessel that can safely navigate only within it. The latter may use the Rule 34(d) doubt signal if in doubt about the crossing vessel's intentions.

(i) In a channel where overtaking can take place only if the vessel to be overtaken must take action to permit safe passing, the overtaking vessel shall signal her intention by Rule 34(c)(i) (two prolonged blasts followed by one short = overtake on your starboard side; followed by two short = on your port side). (ii) The vessel to be overtaken, if she agrees, sounds Rule 34(c)(ii) (prolonged, short, prolonged, short) and takes steps to permit safe passing. If in doubt she may sound the Rule 34(d) signal.
Take particular care and sound the appropriate Rule 34(e) signal when approaching a bend or an area of a narrow channel where other vessels may be hidden by an obstruction.
Any vessel shall, if circumstances allow, avoid anchoring in a narrow channel.

rules.title: Traffic separation schemes
rules.summary: Applies in schemes adopted by IMO. Does not relieve any vessel of her duties under other Rules. Use the correct lane in the general direction of flow, keep clear of the separation zone, join and leave at the ends where practicable, cross at right angles, and avoid anchoring in schemes and near their terminations.

paragraphs.summary: Applies to traffic separation schemes adopted by IMO; does not relieve any vessel of obligations under any other Rule.

A vessel using a scheme shall: (i) proceed in the appropriate traffic lane in the general direction of traffic flow for that lane; (ii) so far as practicable keep clear of a traffic separation line or separation zone; (iii) normally join or leave a lane at the termination, but when joining or leaving from either side do so at as small an angle to the general direction of flow as practicable.
requirements: join/leave at lane ends or at a small angle

paragraphs.summary: A vessel shall, so far as practicable, avoid crossing traffic lanes, but if obliged to do so shall cross as nearly as practicable at right angles to the general direction of traffic flow.

(i) Inshore traffic zones shall not normally be used by through traffic that can safely use the appropriate lane of the adjacent scheme. (ii) Exceptions: vessels of less than 20 m, sailing vessels and vessels engaged in fishing may use the inshore traffic zone. (iii) A vessel may use an inshore zone when en route to or from a port, offshore installation or structure, pilot station or any other place within the zone, or to avoid immediate danger.

A vessel other than a crossing vessel or one joining/leaving a lane shall not normally enter a separation zone or cross a separation line except in emergencies to avoid immediate danger, or to engage in fishing within the zone.
A vessel navigating in areas near the terminations of a scheme shall do so with particular caution.
A vessel shall so far as practicable avoid anchoring in a traffic separation scheme or in areas near its terminations.
A vessel not using a scheme shall avoid it by as wide a margin as is practicable.
A vessel engaged in fishing shall not impede the passage of any vessel following a traffic lane.
A vessel of less than 20 m or a sailing vessel shall not impede the safe passage of a power-driven vessel following a traffic lane.

A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre when engaged in an operation for the maintenance of safety of navigation in a scheme is exempted from this Rule to the extent necessary to carry out the operation.

A vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre when engaged in laying, servicing or picking up a submarine cable within a scheme is exempted from this Rule to the extent necessary to carry out the operation.

simulator_hooks: Crossing a lane: heading within about 10 deg of perpendicular scores compliant; entering the separation zone is flagged.

rules.title: Application (Section II)
rules.summary: Section II rules (Rules 11 to 18) apply to vessels in sight of one another.

rules.title: Sailing vessels
rules.summary: When two sailing vessels approach with risk of collision: the one with the wind on the port side keeps out of the way of the other; if both have it on the same side, the windward vessel keeps clear of the leeward; if a vessel with the wind on the port side cannot tell whether the other has it on port or starboard, she keeps clear.

paragraphs.summary: Wind on different sides: the vessel with the wind on the port side gives way.
Wind on the same side: the windward vessel gives way to the leeward vessel.
If a vessel with wind on the port side sees another to windward and cannot tell if her wind is on port or starboard, she gives way.
The windward side is the side opposite the one on which the mainsail is carried (or, for a square-rigged vessel, opposite the largest fore-and-aft sail).

rules.title: Overtaking
rules.summary: Any vessel overtaking another keeps out of the way of the vessel being overtaken, whatever the other Rules say. A vessel is overtaking when she comes up from more than 22.5 degrees abaft the beam of the other, so that at night she could only see the stern light. If in doubt, assume she is overtaking. The overtaking duty continues until finally past and clear.

paragraphs.summary: Notwithstanding Rules 4-18, any vessel overtaking any other shall keep out of the way of the vessel being overtaken.
A vessel is overtaking when approaching another from a direction more than 22.5 degrees abaft her beam, i.e. in a position where at night she could see only the stern light and neither sidelight.
paragraphs.sector_note: relative bearing of the overtaking vessel from the vessel being overtaken, measured from her bow

paragraphs.summary: If a vessel is in any doubt whether she is overtaking, she shall assume that she is and act accordingly.
A later change in the bearing does not make the overtaking vessel a crossing vessel, nor relieve her of the duty to keep clear until finally past and clear.

simulator_hooks: Overtaking if own bearing from the target is within 112.5-247.5 deg relative to the target's heading.

rules.title: Head-on situation
rules.summary: When two power-driven vessels meet on reciprocal or nearly reciprocal courses so as to involve risk of collision, each alters course to starboard so they pass port to port. A head-on situation exists when each vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead, by day the masts in line or nearly in line and/or both sidelights, by night the masthead lights in line and/or both sidelights. If in doubt, assume it exists.

paragraphs.summary: Each alters course to starboard so each passes on the port side of the other.
Such a situation exists when a vessel sees the other ahead or nearly ahead, by night masthead lights in line or nearly in line and/or both sidelights; by day corresponding aspect.
When a vessel is in any doubt whether such a situation exists, she shall assume that it does exist and act accordingly.

simulator_hooks: Head-on if the target is within a few degrees of dead ahead and her heading is about reciprocal (default head-on sector about +/-6 deg). Port turn is a violation.

rules.title: Crossing situation
rules.summary: When two power-driven vessels cross so as to involve risk of collision, the vessel that has the other on her own starboard side keeps out of the way and, if circumstances allow, avoids crossing ahead of the other.

paragraphs.summary: The vessel with the other on her starboard side keeps out of the way and, if the circumstances admit, avoids crossing ahead of the other vessel.

simulator_hooks: Own gives way if the target lies on the starboard side (relative bearing about 0 to 112.5 deg right of the bow) and she is not head-on or overtaking.

rules.title: Action by give-way vessel
rules.summary: A give-way vessel must take early and substantial action to keep well clear.

paragraphs.summary: Every vessel directed to keep out of the way of another shall, so far as possible, take early and substantial action to keep well clear.

rules.title: Action by stand-on vessel
rules.summary: The stand-on vessel keeps her course and speed. She may act on her own as soon as it is clear the give-way vessel is not taking appropriate action, and must act when collision cannot be avoided by the give-way vessel's action alone. In a crossing situation she must not, if circumstances allow, alter to port for a vessel on her own port side. The give-way vessel's duty is not relieved.

paragraphs.summary: Where one of two vessels is to keep out of the way, the other shall keep her course and speed.
She may however take action to avoid collision by her manoeuvre alone as soon as it becomes apparent that the vessel required to keep out of the way is not taking appropriate action.

When, from any cause, the stand-on vessel finds herself so close that collision cannot be avoided by the action of the give-way vessel alone, she shall take such action as will best aid to avoid collision.

A power-driven vessel taking action in a crossing situation under (a)(ii) to avoid collision with another power-driven vessel shall, if the circumstances admit, not alter course to port for a vessel on her own port side.
This Rule does not relieve the give-way vessel of her obligation to keep out of the way.

keywords: no turn to port in crossing
simulator_hooks: Stage 0 keep course/speed; stage 1 may act; stage 2 must act. Violations: alteration at stage 0, port turn in a crossing at stage 1, no action at stage 2.

rules.title: Responsibilities between vessels
rules.summary: Except where Rules 9, 10 and 13 require otherwise, a hierarchy decides who keeps out of the way.

paragraphs.summary: A power-driven vessel underway keeps out of the way of: (i) a vessel not under command; (ii) a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre; (iii) a vessel engaged in fishing; (iv) a sailing vessel.
A sailing vessel underway keeps out of the way of: (i) a vessel not under command; (ii) a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre; (iii) a vessel engaged in fishing.
A vessel engaged in fishing, when underway, shall so far as possible keep out of the way of: (i) a vessel not under command; (ii) a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre.

(i) Any vessel other than a vessel not under command or restricted in her ability to manoeuvre shall, if circumstances admit, avoid impeding the safe passage of a vessel constrained by her draught exhibiting the Rule 28 signals. (ii) A vessel constrained by her draught shall navigate with particular caution having full regard to her special condition.
A seaplane on the water shall in general keep well clear of all vessels and avoid impeding their navigation; where risk of collision exists she shall comply with these Rules.

(i) A WIG craft when taking off, landing and in flight near the surface shall keep well clear of all other vessels and avoid impeding their navigation. (ii) A WIG craft operating on the water surface shall comply with these Rules as a power-driven vessel.

rules.priority_note: Order from most privileged (kept clear of by all) to least. Each class keeps out of the way of those listed before it, with CBD handled by 18(d) and Rules 9, 10 and 13 overriding.

rules.title: Conduct of vessels in restricted visibility
rules.summary: Applies to vessels not in sight of one another navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility. Proceed at a safe speed with engines ready for immediate manoeuvre; use radar to detect risk; avoid alterations to port for a vessel forward of the beam (other than one being overtaken) and avoid altering toward a vessel abeam or abaft the beam; if a fog signal is heard apparently forward of the beam, or close quarters cannot be avoided, reduce to the minimum speed at which she can be kept on course, and if necessary take all way off, navigating with extreme caution until danger is over.

paragraphs.summary: Applies to vessels not in sight of one another when navigating in or near an area of restricted visibility.
Every vessel shall proceed at a safe speed adapted to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility. A power-driven vessel shall have her engines ready for immediate manoeuvre.
Every vessel shall have due regard to the prevailing circumstances and conditions of restricted visibility when complying with Rules 4 to 10.

A vessel that detects by radar alone another vessel shall determine if a close-quarters situation is developing and/or risk of collision exists; if so she shall take avoiding action in ample time, provided that when such action consists of an alteration of course, so far as possible: (i) an alteration to port for a vessel forward of the beam, other than for a vessel being overtaken, shall be avoided; (ii) an alteration of course towards a vessel abeam or abaft the beam shall be avoided.

prohibited.target_sector: forward of the beam (not being overtaken)

paragraphs.summary: Except where it has been determined that risk of collision does not exist, every vessel that hears apparently forward of her beam the fog signal of another vessel, or can not avoid a close-quarters situation with another vessel forward of her beam, shall reduce speed to the minimum at which she can be kept on her course. She shall if necessary take all her way off and in any event navigate with extreme caution until danger of collision is over.

keywords: no port turn forward of beam
fog signal heard forward of beam
simulator_hooks: Direction rules for avoiding action apply when visibility is below the in-sight range.

rules.title: Application
rules.summary: Rules in Part C are complied with in all weathers. Lights are shown from sunset to sunrise, and in restricted visibility or other necessary circumstances also by day; no other lights that could be mistaken for the prescribed ones or impair their visibility or distinctive character, or interfere with a proper look-out, may be exhibited. Shapes are shown by day.

paragraphs.summary: Part C applies in all weathers.

Lights are exhibited from sunset to sunrise; during that time no other lights shall be shown that cannot be mistaken for the prescribed lights or that impair their visibility, distinctive character or a proper look-out.
Required lights, if carried, are also exhibited from sunrise to sunset in restricted visibility and may be exhibited in all other circumstances when considered necessary.
Rules concerning shapes apply by day.
Lights and shapes must comply with Annex I.

rules.title: Definitions (lights)
rules.summary: Defines the standard navigation lights and their arcs.

lights.name: masthead light
lights.sector: from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam on each side
lights.position: over the fore and aft centreline

lights.name: sidelights
lights.sector: from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam on own side
lights.note: may be combined in one lantern on the centreline on vessels under 20 m

lights.name: sternlight
lights.sector: 67.5 deg each side of right aft

lights.name: flashing light
lights.note: flashes at regular intervals at 120 flashes or more per minute

rules.title: Visibility of lights
rules.summary: Minimum visible ranges, in nautical miles, by vessel length.

L_12_to_under_20.note: masthead 3 nm for 12-20 m; 2 nm for under 12 m

rules.title: Power-driven vessels underway
rules.summary: A power-driven vessel underway shows masthead light(s), sidelights and sternlight. Special additions for air-cushion vessels, small craft and under-12 m vessels.

paragraphs.summary: (i) A masthead light forward; (ii) a second masthead light abaft and higher than the forward one (vessels under 50 m need not show it but may); (iii) sidelights; (iv) a sternlight.

lights.arc: 225 deg, from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam each side
225 deg, from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam each side
lights.note: aft and higher; mandatory for 50 m or more

lights.arc: 112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, starboard side
112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, port side

paragraphs.summary: An air-cushion vessel in non-displacement mode also exhibits an all-round flashing yellow light.
A WIG craft only when taking off, landing and in flight near the surface also exhibits a high-intensity all-round flashing red light.

A power-driven vessel of less than 12 m may instead show an all-round white light and sidelights. A power-driven vessel under 7 m whose maximum speed does not exceed 7 knots may show only an all-round white light and, if practicable, sidelights. The masthead or all-round light on a vessel under 12 m may be displaced from the centreline if centreline fitting is impracticable, provided the sidelights are combined in one lantern on the centreline.

rules.title: Towing and pushing
rules.summary: Power-driven vessel towing or pushing shows extra masthead lights, a yellow towing light above the sternlight, and a diamond shape by day when the tow exceeds 200 m.

paragraphs.summary: Power-driven vessel when towing astern: two masthead lights in a vertical line instead of one (three if the tow measured from the stern of the tug to the after end of the tow exceeds 200 m), sidelights, a sternlight, a towing light in a vertical line above the sternlight, and a diamond shape where it can best be seen if the tow exceeds 200 m.

lights.arc: 225 deg, from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam each side
lights.note: 3 if the length of tow exceeds 200 m

lights.arc: 112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, starboard side
112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, port side
135 deg, vertical line above the sternlight

paragraphs.day_shape: diamond where best seen if the tow exceeds 200 m

paragraphs.summary: Pushing ahead or towing alongside, when rigidly connected as a composite unit, is treated as a single power-driven vessel (Rule 23).
A power-driven vessel pushing ahead or towing alongside (not a composite unit) shows two masthead lights in a vertical line, sidelights and a sternlight.
A power-driven vessel to which (a) or (c) applies must also comply with Rule 23(a)(ii).
A vessel or object being towed other than as in (g) shows sidelights, a sternlight and, if the tow exceeds 200 m, a diamond shape where best seen.

Any number of vessels towed alongside or pushed in a group are lit as one vessel; a vessel pushed ahead (not part of a composite unit) shows sidelights at the forward end; a vessel towed alongside shows a sternlight and sidelights at the forward end.

An inconspicuous, partly submerged vessel or object, or combination, being towed shows (i) if less than 25 m wide, one all-round white light at or near each end; (ii) if 25 m or more wide, two additional all-round white lights at or near the extremities of her breadth; (iii) if over 100 m long, additional all-round white lights so the distance between lights does not exceed 100 m; (iv) a diamond shape at or near the aftermost extremity of the last vessel or object towed and, if the tow exceeds 200 m, an additional diamond where best seen and as far forward as practicable.

Where it is impracticable for a vessel or object towed to show the lights of (e) or (g), all possible measures shall be taken to light the vessel or object towed or at least indicate the presence of the unlighted vessel or object.

Where it is impracticable for a vessel not normally engaged in towing operations to show the lights of (a) or (c), she is not required to show them when towing another vessel in distress or otherwise in need of assistance; all possible measures shall be taken to indicate the relationship between the towing vessel and the vessel being assisted, in particular the towline being illuminated.

rules.title: Sailing vessels underway and vessels under oars
rules.summary: Sailing vessel underway shows sidelights and a sternlight; under 20 m the sidelights and sternlight may be combined in one lantern at the masthead. Optional red-over-green all-round lights at the masthead (not with the combined lantern). A vessel under sail and machinery shows a conical shape apex down forward. Under 7 m or oars shows a torch or white light.

paragraphs.summary: Sailing vessel underway: sidelights and a sternlight.

lights.arc: 112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, starboard side
112.5 deg from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam, port side

paragraphs.summary: On a sailing vessel under 20 m, the lights of (a) may be combined in one lantern carried at or near the top of the mast where it can best be seen.

A sailing vessel underway may in addition exhibit, at or near the top of the mast, where best seen, two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper red and the lower green; not together with the combined lantern in (b).

(i) A sailing vessel of less than 7 m shall, if practicable, show the lights of (a) or (b); if not, she shall have ready at hand an electric torch or lighted lantern showing a white light, exhibited in sufficient time to prevent collision. (ii) A vessel under oars may show the lights of this Rule or have ready at hand a torch or lighted lantern showing a white light.
A vessel proceeding under sail when also being propelled by machinery shall exhibit forward where best seen a conical shape, apex downwards.

rules.title: Fishing vessels
rules.summary: A vessel engaged in fishing, underway or at anchor, shows only the lights and shapes of this Rule. Trawlers show green over white all-round; other fishing vessels red over white; a cone (apex up) or basket by day. Sidelights and sternlight only when making way. Extra white all-round light towards outlying gear over 150 m.

paragraphs.summary: Applies to vessels engaged in fishing, whether underway or at anchor; only the lights and shapes prescribed here are shown.

Trawling (dragging a dredge net or other apparatus): two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper green and the lower white, or a shape of two cones with apexes together in a vertical line one above the other; a masthead light abaft and higher than the green light (vessels under 50 m may but need not show it); when making way through the water, sidelights and a sternlight too.

lights.arc: 225 deg, from right ahead to 22.5 deg abaft the beam each side
lights.note: abaft and higher than the green light; optional under 50 m

lights: sidelights and sternlight when making way

paragraphs.summary: Fishing other than trawling: two all-round lights in a vertical line, the upper red and the lower white, or a shape of two cones apexes together; where outlying gear extends more than 150 m horizontally, an all-round white light or a cone apex up in the direction of the gear; when making way, sidelights and a sternlight too.
paragraphs.day_shape: two cones apexes together; cone apex up towards outlying gear > 150 m

paragraphs.summary: Additional signals for fishing vessels fishing in close proximity are in Annex II.
A vessel not engaged in fishing shall not show the lights or shapes of this Rule, but only those of her length class.

rules.title: Vessels not under command or restricted in their ability to manoeuvre
rules.summary: NUC: two all-round reds vertical (two black balls by day). RAM: red-white-red vertical (ball-diamond-ball by day). Dredging or underwater work adds red-red on the obstructed side and green-green on the safe-passing side (balls / diamonds by day). Mine clearance adds three all-round green lights/balls. Diving: rigid replica of the flag A.

paragraphs.summary: Vessel not under command: two all-round red lights in a vertical line where best seen; two balls or similar shapes in a vertical line by day; when making way, sidelights and a sternlight too.
lights: sidelights and sternlight only when making way

paragraphs.summary: Vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre (except mine clearance): three all-round lights in a vertical line, the highest and lowest red and the middle white; by day three shapes in a vertical line, the highest and lowest balls and the middle a diamond; when making way, masthead lights, sidelights and a sternlight; when at anchor, in addition to these, the anchor light(s) or shape of Rule 30.

A power-driven vessel engaged in a towing operation that severely restricts the towing vessel and her tow from deviating shall, in addition to Rule 24(a) lights/shapes, exhibit the lights or shapes of (b).

A vessel engaged in dredging or underwater operations, when restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, shall show the (b) lights and shapes and, in addition, when an obstruction exists: two all-round red lights or two balls in a vertical line to indicate the side on which the obstruction exists; two all-round green lights or two diamonds in a vertical line to indicate the side on which another vessel may pass; when at anchor, the lights/shapes of this paragraph instead of Rule 30.
paragraphs.day_shape: two balls on the obstructed side; two diamonds on the safe-passing side

paragraphs.summary: A vessel engaged in diving operations that is too small to show the lights and shapes of (b) and (d) shall show three all-round lights red-white-red in a vertical line, a rigid replica of the International Code flag 'A' at least 1 m high, and all-round measures to ensure it is visible.
paragraphs.day_shape: rigid replica of flag A, at least 1 m high

paragraphs.summary: A vessel engaged in mine clearance, in addition to the Rule 23 lights for a power-driven vessel or the Rule 30 anchor lights/shape, shows three all-round green lights or three balls; one near the foremast head and one at each end of the fore yard; these signals mean it is dangerous for another vessel to approach within 1000 m of the mine-clearance vessel.
Vessels under 12 m (other than diving vessels) are not required to show the lights and shapes of this Rule.
The signals in this Rule are not distress signals (see Annex IV).

rules.title: Vessels constrained by their draught
rules.summary: A vessel constrained by her draught may, in addition to Rule 23 lights, show three all-round red lights in a vertical line, or a cylinder by day.

paragraphs.summary: May show three all-round red lights vertical, or a cylinder.

rules.title: Pilot vessels
rules.summary: Pilot vessel on pilotage duty: two all-round lights, white over red, at or near the masthead; sidelights and sternlight when underway; anchor light(s) when at anchor. Not on pilotage duty: lights of her class.

paragraphs.summary: On pilotage duty: white over red all-round at masthead; underway, sidelights and sternlight; at anchor, anchor lights or shape too.
When not engaged on pilotage duty, she shows the lights or shapes for a vessel of her length.

rules.title: Anchored vessels and vessels aground
rules.summary: Anchored vessel: forward all-round white light or one ball; at 50 m or more a second all-round white aft and lower; deck lights optional (required at 100 m or more). Aground: anchor lights plus two all-round red vertical (three balls by day).

paragraphs.summary: Anchored: (i) in the fore part, an all-round white light or one ball; (ii) at or near the stern and lower than the forward light, an all-round white light.
A vessel of less than 50 m may show an all-round white light where best seen instead of the two lights of (a).
A vessel at anchor may, and a vessel of 100 m or more shall, also use available working or equivalent lights to illuminate her decks.
Aground: the (a) or (b) lights and, where best seen, two all-round red lights in a vertical line, or three balls in a vertical line by day.
Vessels under 7 m not in or near a narrow channel, fairway, anchorage or where other vessels normally navigate need not show these lights or shape.
Vessels under 12 m aground need not show the aground lights or shapes of (d).

rules.title: Seaplanes
rules.summary: Where it is impracticable for a seaplane or WIG craft on the water to show lights and shapes of the Part C characteristics, she shows lights and shapes as closely similar as possible.

paragraphs.summary: Show lights and shapes as closely similar in characteristics and position as is possible.

rules.title: Definitions (sound signals)
rules.summary: Defines the sound signals.

definitions.meaning: any sound-signalling appliance capable of producing the prescribed blasts and complying with Annex III
a blast of about one second's duration
a blast of four to six seconds' duration

rules.title: Equipment for sound signals
rules.summary: Vessels of 12 m or more carry a whistle; 20 m or more also a bell; 100 m or more also a gong whose tone cannot be confused with the bell. Vessels under 12 m need not carry them but must have some other means of making an efficient sound signal.

paragraphs.summary: 12 m or more: whistle; 20 m or more: also a bell; 100 m or more: also a gong (tone distinct from the bell). All comply with Annex III. Bell and gong may be replaced by equipment with the same sound characteristics provided manual sounding is always possible.
Under 12 m: not obliged to carry these, but must then have some other means of making an efficient sound signal.

rules.title: Manoeuvring and warning signals
rules.summary: Signals for vessels in sight of one another when manoeuvring, overtaking, in doubt, or at blind bends. Light signals may supplement the whistle.

paragraphs.summary: When power-driven vessels are in sight of one another and manoeuvring as authorised or required by the Rules, the manoeuvre is indicated by whistle signals.

signals.meaning: I am altering my course to starboard
I am altering my course to port

paragraphs.summary: A vessel may supplement the whistle signals with light signals, repeated as appropriate while the manoeuvre is carried out: flashes mean the same as the blasts; each flash about one second long, interval about one second between flashes, interval between successive signals at least ten seconds. The light, if fitted, is an all-round white light visible at least 5 miles, complying with Annex I.

In a narrow channel or fairway (see Rule 9(e)): the overtaking vessel signals her intention. Two prolonged then one short = I intend to overtake on your starboard side. Two prolonged then two short = I intend to overtake on your port side. The vessel about to be overtaken, if in agreement, sounds prolonged, short, prolonged, short.

signals.meaning: I intend to overtake you on your starboard side
I intend to overtake you on your port side

paragraphs.summary: When vessels in sight of one another are approaching and either vessel fails to understand the intentions or actions of the other, or is in doubt whether sufficient action is being taken to avoid collision, she shall immediately indicate doubt by at least five short and rapid blasts, which may be supplemented by at least five short and rapid flashes.

A vessel nearing a bend or an area of a channel or fairway where other vessels may be hidden by an obstruction shall sound one prolonged blast. Any approaching vessel that hears it answers with a prolonged blast.

signals.meaning: approaching a bend; answered by 1 prolonged blast

paragraphs.summary: If whistles are fitted on a vessel more than 100 m apart, only one whistle is used for giving manoeuvring and warning signals.

rules.title: Sound signals in restricted visibility
rules.summary: In or near an area of restricted visibility, by day or night: signals are made at intervals of not more than 2 minutes (1 minute for the anchored/aground bell).

paragraphs.summary: Power-driven vessel making way through the water: one prolonged blast at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
Power-driven vessel underway but stopped and making no way through the water: two prolonged blasts in succession, about 2 seconds apart, at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.

Vessel not under command, restricted in her ability to manoeuvre, constrained by her draught, sailing, engaged in fishing, or engaged in towing or pushing: instead of (a) or (b), one prolonged blast followed by two short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
paragraphs.vessel: NUC, RAM, CBD, sailing, fishing, towing or pushing

paragraphs.summary: A vessel engaged in fishing when at anchor, and a vessel restricted in her ability to manoeuvre when carrying out her work at anchor, sound the (c) signal instead of the anchor signal of (g).
paragraphs.vessel: fishing at anchor; RAM working at anchor

paragraphs.summary: A vessel towed, or the last vessel of a tow if manned: one prolonged followed by three short blasts at intervals of not more than 2 minutes, made where practicable immediately after the towing vessel's signal.
A pushing vessel and the vessel pushed ahead, rigidly connected as a composite unit, are regarded as one power-driven vessel and give the (a) or (b) signals.

Vessel at anchor: rapid ringing of the bell for about 5 seconds at intervals of not more than 1 minute. A vessel of 100 m or more rings the bell forward and immediately after sounds the gong rapidly for about 5 seconds aft. She may in addition sound one short, one prolonged and one short blast to warn an approaching vessel of her position and of the possibility of collision.
paragraphs.signal: bell about 5 s (gong aft for 100 m or more); optional S-L-S

paragraphs.summary: Vessel aground: the bell (and gong if required) signal of (g) and, in addition, three separate and distinct strokes on the bell immediately before and after the rapid ringing. She may in addition sound an appropriate whistle signal.
paragraphs.signal: 3 strokes + rapid bell about 5 s + 3 strokes

paragraphs.summary: A vessel of 12 m or more but less than 20 m is not obliged to give the bell signals of (g) and (h) but, if she does not, must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
A vessel of less than 12 m is not obliged to give the above signals but, if she does not, must make some other efficient sound signal at intervals of not more than 2 minutes.
A pilot vessel engaged on pilotage duty may, in addition to the (a), (b) or (g) signals, sound an identity signal of four short blasts.

rules.title: Signals to attract attention
rules.summary: Any vessel may make light or sound signals that cannot be mistaken for any signal authorised elsewhere in the Rules, or may direct the beam of her searchlight in the direction of the danger so as not to embarrass any vessel. Avoid high-intensity intermittent or revolving lights such as strobe lights.

paragraphs.summary: Attention-getting light or sound signals are allowed if not confusable with Rule signals; a searchlight may be pointed toward the danger without dazzling other vessels; avoid strobe-type lights.

rules.title: Distress signals
rules.summary: A vessel in distress and requiring assistance uses or exhibits the signals described in Annex IV.

rules.title: Exemptions
rules.summary: Vessels that complied with the 1960 Regulations and whose keel was laid (or at a corresponding stage) before entry into force of the 1972 Regulations were exempted from certain requirements: range and colour specifications of lights for 4 years; repositioning of lights from metric conversion permanently; repositioning of masthead lights under Annex I 3(a) permanent for under 150 m and 9 years for 150 m or more; repositioning of masthead lights (Annex I 2(b)), sidelights (2(g), 3(b)), all-round lights (9(b)) and sound-signal appliances (Annex III) for 9 years. No longer practically relevant.

rules.title: Definitions (verification of compliance)
rules.summary: Audit; Audit Scheme (IMO Member State Audit Scheme); Code for Implementation (III Code, resolution A.1070(28)); Audit Standard (the Code for Implementation).

definitions.meaning: systematic, independent, documented process of obtaining evidence and evaluating it objectively against audit criteria
IMO Member State Audit Scheme
IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code), resolution A.1070(28)
the Code for Implementation

rules.title: Application (Part F)
rules.summary: Contracting Parties use the provisions of the Code for Implementation in carrying out their obligations and responsibilities under the Convention.

rules.title: Verification of compliance
rules.summary: Every Contracting Party is subject to periodic IMO audits against the audit standard; the Secretary-General administers the audit scheme; each Party facilitates the audit and implements a programme of action on findings; audits follow an overall schedule at periodic intervals.

paragraphs.summary: Periodic IMO audits of each Contracting Party against the audit standard.
Secretary-General administers the Audit Scheme.
Each Party facilitates the audit and acts on findings.
Audits follow a Secretary-General schedule and run at periodic intervals.

night: sternlight (or tricolour at masthead under 20 m)
optional red over green all-round (not with tricolour)

vessel_lights_and_shapes_catalogue.vessel: Tug towing astern, tow 200 m or less
Tug towing astern, tow over 200 m

night: masthead abaft and higher (optional under 50 m)
sidelights and sternlight if making way
extra white all-round toward gear over 150 m
sidelights and sternlight if making way
day: cone apex up toward gear over 150 m

night: sidelights and sternlight if making way
deck lights (required at 100 m or more)

annexes.title: Positioning and technical details of lights and shapes

sections.title: Definition
sections.summary: 'Height above the hull' means height above the uppermost continuous deck, measured vertically beneath the light.

sections.title: Vertical positioning and spacing of lights

items.summary: Power-driven vessel 20 m or more: forward masthead light at least 6 m above the hull (and, if breadth exceeds 6 m, at least the breadth, but need not exceed 12 m); when two masthead lights are carried the after one is at least 4.5 m higher than the forward one.
Vertical separation is such that in normal trim the after light is seen over and separate from the forward light at 1,000 m from the stem, viewed from sea level.
Power-driven vessel 12 m to under 20 m: masthead light at least 2.5 m above the gunwale.

Power-driven vessel under 12 m may carry the uppermost light lower than 2.5 m above the gunwale; but if a masthead or all-round light is carried together with sidelights and sternlight, it is at least 1 m higher than the sidelights.

One of the two or three masthead lights of a towing/pushing vessel is in the same position as the forward or after masthead light; if on the aftermast, the lowest after masthead light is at least 4.5 m above the forward one.

Masthead lights are above and clear of all other lights and obstructions, except that all-round lights of Rules 27(b)(i) and 28 may be carried above the after masthead light(s) or between the forward and after masthead lights (then Section 3(c) applies).
Sidelights of a power-driven vessel are at a height not greater than three quarters of the forward masthead light and not so low as to be interfered with by deck lights.
Combined-lantern sidelights on a power-driven vessel under 20 m are at least 1 m below the masthead light.

Two or three vertical lights are spaced at least 2 m apart on vessels 20 m or more (lowest at least 4 m above the hull, except towing light), at least 1 m apart on vessels under 20 m (lowest at least 2 m above the gunwale); three lights are equally spaced.
Lower of the two all-round fishing lights is above the sidelights by at least twice the distance between the two vertical lights.
Forward anchor light, when two are carried, is at least 4.5 m above the after one; on a vessel of 50 m or more it is at least 6 m above the hull.

sections.title: Horizontal positioning and spacing of lights

items.summary: Two masthead lights: horizontal distance at least half the vessel's length (no more than 100 m); the forward light not more than a quarter of the length from the stem.
Vessel 20 m or more: sidelights are not in front of the forward masthead lights and are at or near the side.
When Rule 27(b)(i)/28 all-round lights are placed between the masthead lights, they are at least 2 m from the fore-and-aft centreline athwartships.
When only one masthead light is prescribed, it is exhibited forward of amidships; a vessel under 20 m need not exhibit it forward of amidships but as far forward as practicable.

sections.title: Direction-indicating lights for fishing vessels, dredgers and vessels in underwater operations

items.summary: Fishing: the light showing the direction of outlying gear (Rule 26(c)(ii)) is 2 m to 6 m horizontally away from the two all-round red and white lights, not higher than the all-round white light and not lower than the sidelights.

Dredging/underwater operations: obstruction/safe-side lights and shapes of Rule 27(d) are at the maximum practical horizontal distance, never less than 2 m, from the Rule 27(b) lights/shapes; the upper is never higher than the lower of the three Rule 27(b) lights/shapes.

sections.title: Screens for sidelights
sections.summary: Sidelights of vessels of 20 m or more are fitted with inboard matt black screens; under 20 m only if needed to meet the sector requirements. A combined lantern with a single vertical filament and a very narrow division needs no external screens.

items.summary: Shapes are black. Ball: diameter at least 0.6 m. Cone: base diameter at least 0.6 m, height equal to the diameter. Cylinder: diameter at least 0.6 m, height twice the diameter. Diamond: two cones with a common base.
Vertical distance between shapes is at least 1.5 m.
Vessels under 20 m may use smaller shapes commensurate with their size, with correspondingly reduced spacing.

sections.title: Colour specification of lights
sections.summary: Chromaticity of navigation lights must lie within the CIE chromaticity-diagram areas for white, green, red and yellow (corner coordinates given in the Annex).

sections.title: Intensity of lights
sections.summary: Minimum luminous intensity I = 3.43 x 10^6 x T x D^2 x K^-D candela, with threshold T = 2 x 10^-7 lux, D the luminous range in nautical miles and K = 0.8 (atmospheric transmissivity, about 13 nm meteorological visibility). Maximum intensity should be limited to avoid glare, not by a variable control.

items.summary: Forward direction: sidelights show minimum required intensity forward; intensities decrease to practical cut-off between 1 and 3 degrees outside the prescribed sectors.

Sternlights, masthead lights and sidelights at 22.5 degrees abaft the beam: minimum intensity maintained to 5 degrees within the sector limits, may fall 50 per cent up to the limit, and reaches cut-off within 5 degrees outside the sector.
All-round lights are not obscured by masts or structures over more than 6 degrees of arc (anchor lights excepted).
If impracticable with a single all-round light, use two suitably positioned or screened to appear as one at 1 mile.

Electric lights (other than on sailing vessels underway): at least the required minimum intensity from 5 degrees above to 5 degrees below the horizontal; at least 60 per cent from 7.5 degrees above to 7.5 degrees below.
Sailing vessels underway: minimum intensity from 5 degrees above to 5 degrees below the horizontal; at least 50 per cent from 25 degrees above to 25 degrees below.
Non-electric lights meet these specifications as closely as possible.

sections.title: Intensity of non-electric lights
sections.summary: Non-electric lights comply as far as practicable with the minimum intensities in the Section 8 table.

sections.title: Manoeuvring light
sections.summary: The Rule 34(b) manoeuvring light is in the same fore-and-aft vertical plane as the masthead light(s) and, where practicable, at least 2 m vertically above the forward masthead light; at least 2 m vertically above or below the after masthead light; with a single masthead light it is at least 2 m from it.

sections.title: High-speed craft
sections.summary: The masthead light of high-speed craft may be lower than normal provided the angle subtended by the sidelights and masthead light satisfies the Annex; on high-speed craft of 50 m or more the 4.5 m vertical separation of masthead lights may be reduced according to the Annex formula.

sections.title: Approval
sections.summary: Construction and installation of lights and shapes must satisfy the flag State's appropriate authority.

annexes.title: Additional signals for fishing vessels fishing in close proximity

sections.title: General
sections.summary: Lights are exhibited under Rule 26(d), placed where best seen, at least 0.9 m apart and lower than the Rule 26(b)(i) and (c)(i) lights; they are visible all round the horizon at least 1 mile but less than the distance prescribed for fishing-vessel lights.

items.summary: Trawling vessels of 20 m or more (demersal or pelagic gear): shooting nets = two white lights in a vertical line; hauling nets = white over red; net fast on an obstruction = two red lights in a vertical line.
Pair trawling, 20 m or more: by night a searchlight directed forward toward the other vessel of the pair; plus the (a) signals when shooting, hauling or fast.
Trawlers under 20 m (single or pair) may exhibit the (a) or (b) signals.

sections.title: Signals for purse seiners
sections.summary: Vessels fishing with purse seines may show two yellow lights in a vertical line, flashing alternately every second with equal light and occultation, only when hampered by their fishing gear.

signals.lights: two yellow, flashing alternately every second

annexes.title: Technical details of sound signal appliances

items.summary: Fundamental frequency within 70-700 Hz. Audibility range is determined by frequencies within 180-700 Hz (+/-1 per cent) for vessels of 20 m or more, or 180-2100 Hz for vessels under 20 m.
Fundamental frequency limits: 70-200 Hz for 200 m or more; 130-350 Hz for 75 m to under 200 m; 250-700 Hz for under 75 m.

Sound pressure level at 1 m in the axis direction (1/3-octave band): 143 dB for 200 m or more (audibility about 2 nm); 138 dB for 75 to under 200 m (1.5 nm); 130 dB for 20 to under 75 m (1 nm); 120 dB for under 20 m (0.5 nm). The Annex table carries footnotes for measured frequencies in the 180-450, 450-800 and 800-2100 Hz ranges.

Directional whistle: level not more than 4 dB below the axis level within +/-45 degrees of the axis, and not more than 10 dB below in any other horizontal direction (range at least half the forward range).

A directional whistle used alone is installed with maximum intensity straight ahead; whistles are placed as high as practicable; own-signal level at listening posts should not exceed 110 dB(A) and preferably 100 dB(A).
Whistles more than 100 m apart must not sound simultaneously.
Combined whistle system counts as a single whistle: whistles within 100 m of each other, sounded together, frequencies differing by at least 10 Hz.
Sound pressure level of at least 110 dB at 1 m.

Corrosion-resistant material with a clear tone; bell mouth diameter at least 300 mm for vessels of 20 m or more; a power-driven striker is recommended but manual operation must be possible; striker mass at least 3 per cent of the bell mass.

sections.title: Approval
sections.summary: Construction, performance and installation of sound appliances satisfy the flag State's appropriate authority.

sections.title: Signals indicating distress and need of assistance
sections.summary: Used or exhibited together or separately.
signals: a gun or other explosive signal fired at intervals of about a minute
continuous sounding with any fog-signalling apparatus
rockets or shells throwing red stars, fired one at a time at short intervals
a signal made by any signalling method consisting of the group ... --- ... (SOS) in Morse
a radiotelephone signal consisting of the spoken word MAYDAY
the International Code Signal of distress indicated by N.C.
a signal consisting of a square flag having above or below it a ball or anything resembling a ball
flames on the vessel (as from a burning tar barrel, oil barrel, etc.)
a rocket parachute flare or a hand flare showing a red light
a smoke signal giving off orange-coloured smoke
slowly and repeatedly raising and lowering arms outstretched to each side
a distress alert by DSC on VHF channel 70, or on MF/HF at 2187.5, 8414.5, 4207.5, 6312, 12577 or 16804.5 kHz
a ship-to-shore distress alert by Inmarsat or another mobile satellite service ship earth station
signals transmitted by emergency position-indicating radio beacons (EPIRB)
approved signals by radiocommunication systems, including survival craft radar transponders

sections.title: Prohibition
sections.summary: Using or exhibiting any of these signals except to indicate distress and need of assistance, and using other signals that could be confused with them, is prohibited.

sections.title: Other aids noted
sections.summary: Attention is drawn to the International Code of Signals and the IAMSAR Manual Volume III; also a piece of orange canvas with a black square and circle (for identification from the air) and a dye marker.

imo_guidance.title: IMO guidance for the uniform application of certain Rules of the 1972 Collision Regulations

items.summary: Both depth of water and available navigable width decide whether a vessel is constrained by her draught, along with the effect of small under-keel clearance on manoeuvrability. A vessel with small under-keel clearance but adequate room to avoid should not be regarded as constrained by her draught.
Apply the definition together with Rule 35(b): a vessel may be underway but stopped and making no way through the water.

A vessel required not to impede another's passage must, so far as practicable, navigate so as to avoid the development of risk of collision. If risk of collision does develop, the relevant steering and sailing rules must be complied with.

items.rule: R10 with Part B Sections II and III
items.summary: A vessel in or near an IMO scheme complies with Rule 10 to minimise risk of collision; all other Rules still apply in full, in particular Part B Sections II and III, once risk of collision exists.
Moving from one side of a lane to the other is ordinary prudent seamanship, provided it is done at as small an angle to the general direction of traffic flow as practicable.

items.topic: Inshore traffic zones for small vessels
items.summary: A vessel under 20 m or a sailing vessel, even when through traffic, may use inshore traffic zones, to comply with Rule 10(j) and for safe navigation.

items.topic: CBD and the steering and sailing rules
items.summary: A vessel constrained by her draught applies the relevant steering and sailing rules as a power-driven vessel when risk of collision exists in a crossing or head-on situation. When showing Rule 28 signals she should have engines ready for immediate manoeuvre and proceed at a safe speed.

traffic_separation_schemes.title: Ships' routeing and traffic separation schemes
objectives: separate opposing streams of traffic to reduce head-on encounters
reduce collision danger between crossing traffic and shipping in established lanes
simplify traffic patterns in converging areas
organise safe flow in areas of offshore exploration or exploitation
keep traffic clear of areas where navigation is dangerous or undesirable
reduce grounding risk by guiding deep-draught vessels where depths are critical
guide traffic clear of, or through, fishing grounds

definitions.meaning: Any system of routes and/or routeing measures aimed at reducing casualties: TSS, two-way routes, recommended tracks, areas to be avoided, inshore traffic zones, roundabouts, precautionary areas and deep water routes.
A routeing measure separating opposing streams of traffic by appropriate means and by establishing traffic lanes.
A zone or line separating traffic lanes in opposite or nearly opposite directions, or a lane from the adjacent inshore traffic zone.
An area within defined limits in which one-way traffic is established.
A separation point or circular separation zone with a circular traffic lane; traffic moves counterclockwise around it.
Designated area between the landward boundary of a TSS and the adjacent coast, intended for local traffic.
A route within defined limits with two-way traffic, for safe passage through difficult or dangerous waters.
A route specially examined to be as free of dangers as possible, along which ships are advised to navigate.
A route within defined limits accurately surveyed for clearance of the sea bottom and submerged obstacles.
An area within defined limits where ships must navigate with particular caution and where the direction of traffic flow may be recommended.
An area where navigation is particularly hazardous or it is exceptionally important to avoid casualties; to be avoided by all ships or certain classes.
Directional movement of traffic established within a TSS.
A recommended directional movement within a routeing system where an established direction is impractical or unnecessary.

traffic_separation_schemes.imo_role: IMO is the only international body responsible for establishing and recommending routeing measures; it will not adopt or amend a system affecting a coastal State's resource rights, environment or traffic without that State's agreement.
conduct_synopsis: Use of a TSS is recommended, not mandatory, but a vessel not using one avoids it by a wide margin (Rule 10(h)).
Keep to the right side of the lane (follow the flow arrows; no need to steer exactly along them).
Join or leave lanes at the terminations; if from the side, at as small an angle as practicable.
Keep clear of separation zones and lines except when crossing, joining or leaving a lane, fishing, or in an emergency.

If a lane must be crossed, do it as nearly as practicable at right angles, whether or not other ships are present; special circumstances (clearing another vessel, weather, wind for sailing vessels) may justify less.
Never anchor in a lane, a separation zone or near the terminations.

Inshore traffic zones are for local traffic; through traffic does not use them, except vessels under 20 m and sailing vessels, vessels bound to or from a port, pilot station or offshore installation inside the zone, and to avoid immediate danger.
Fishing vessels may fish in a separation zone but must not impede lane traffic and should keep gear inside the zone.
Deep water routes (marked DW) are for vessels constrained by draught showing the required signals.
Cable layers, mark layers and survey vessels are RAM and exempted from Rule 10 only to the extent necessary for their work.
International Code signal YG means: you appear not to be complying with the traffic separation scheme.
Normal steering and sailing rules still apply whenever risk of collision develops.
chart_conventions: separation lines or zones between opposing lanes
staggered arrows show established or recommended flow
single arrow = one-way track, opposed arrows = two-way track
continuous arrow line = track based on fixed marks; dashed = not based on fixed marks
letters DW on deep water routes

iala_buoyage.title: IALA Maritime Buoyage System
iala_buoyage.history: Over thirty conflicting systems existed in 1976; IALA combined Systems A (red to port) and B (red to starboard) into one set of rules in 1980 with two regions.

regions.A: Red to port, green to starboard when entering from seaward. Most of the world: Europe, Africa, Australia, New Zealand, the Gulf and most of Asia.
regions.B: Red to starboard, green to port when entering from seaward. The Americas, Japan, Korea and the Philippines.

iala_buoyage.conventional_direction_of_buoyage: General direction taken when approaching a harbour, river, estuary or waterway from seaward, or as decided by the authority; in principle clockwise around land masses.

starboard.light: green, any rhythm other than composite group flashing (2+1)

preferred_channel_to_starboard.colour: red with one broad green horizontal band

preferred_channel_to_port.colour: green with one broad red horizontal band

preferred_channel_to_starboard.colour: green with one broad red band

preferred_channel_to_port.colour: red with one broad green band

cardinal.note: Show where the deepest water lies, named side of the mark. Yellow and black bands, black double-cone topmarks, white lights VQ or Q. Pillar or spar; no distinctive shape. Topmark points show where the black band lies.

east.light: VQ(3) every 5 s or Q(3) every 10 s

south.light: VQ(6)+LFl every 10 s or Q(6)+LFl every 15 s

stcw_watchkeeping.title: STCW (as amended, Manila 2010) - extracts for watchkeeping
structure_in_book: Chapter I general provisions: definitions, certificates, near-coastal voyages, control procedures, training and assessment, quality standards, medical standards, simulators, company responsibilities, transitional provisions
Chapter II master and deck department: certification of officers in charge of a navigational watch, masters and chief mates, ratings forming part of a navigational watch, able seafarer deck
Chapter IV radiocommunication and GMDSS radio operators
Chapter V special training for tanker and passenger ship personnel

exceptions.note: exceptions may not extend beyond two 24-hour periods in any 7-day period

voyage_planning: master ensures the route from departure port to first port of call is planned on adequate, up-to-date charts and publications
planned route is displayed on charts and verified by the officer of the watch before each course is followed
an amended route is planned before any substantial deviation
watchkeeping_principles: The OOW is the master's representative and is primarily responsible for safe navigation and for complying with the Collision Regulations.
A proper look-out is kept at all times in compliance with Rule 5; the OOW does not hand over lookout responsibility.
Use radar whenever restricted visibility is encountered or expected and always in congested waters; change range scales often; start plotting early.
Take frequent, accurate compass bearings of approaching ships; risk can exist despite appreciable bearing change; take early positive action and check its effect.
Know the ship's handling characteristics including stopping distance; remember other ships differ.
Do not hesitate to use helm, engines and sound signals; give timely notice of engine changes where possible.
Put the steering to manual in good time; relying on auto-pilot until help is needed is dangerous.
Test navigational equipment at sea before hazardous conditions and before arrival and departure; check compass error each watch.
A pilot on board does not relieve the master or OOW of their duties; query the pilot's actions and call the master if in doubt.
At anchor: plot position, monitor bearings for dragging, keep a look-out, show anchor lights and shapes, sound fog signals when needed.
call_the_master_when: restricted visibility is encountered or expected
traffic conditions or other ships' movements cause concern
land, a mark or soundings are not seen when expected, or appear unexpectedly
breakdown of engines, propulsion controls, steering gear or essential navigational equipment
heavy weather and doubt about damage
a hazard to navigation such as ice or a derelict is met
in any other emergency or in any doubt
restricted_visibility_actions: comply with the Collision Regulations, especially fog signals, safe speed and engines ready for manoeuvre
stcw_watchkeeping.radio_watch: Part 4-3 principles for keeping a radio watch and Part B guidance cover distress, urgency and safety communications.

encounter_classification.relative_bearing_convention: bearing of the other vessel from own ship, measured clockwise from own bow, 0-360
steps: 1. Is risk of collision present? (R7) closing range and CPA below the CPA limit, or constant bearing; doubt means yes
2. If either vessel is NUC, RAM, fishing, sailing, CBD: apply R18 priority (and R9/R10/R13 first where they apply)
3. Overtaking? (R13) other vessel is within the 112.5-247.5 deg sector of the vessel being overtaken = overtaking vessel gives way
4. Head-on? (R14) both power-driven, each sees the other ahead or nearly ahead, courses reciprocal or nearly reciprocal = both alter to starboard
5. Crossing? (R15) the vessel with the other on her starboard side (0 to 112.5 deg right of the bow) gives way
6. Sailing vs sailing: R12 (port tack gives way; same tack windward gives way)
7. In restricted visibility and not in sight: R19 (no turn to port for a target forward of the beam except an overtaken vessel; no turn toward a target abeam or abaft)

roles.HO: head-on, both give way to starboard (R14)

special_cases: CBD: others avoid impeding her passage (R18(d)); she acts as a power-driven vessel in crossing/head-on
Overtaking (R13), narrow channel (R9) and TSS (R10) override the R18 order
Seaplane / WIG on water: keep well clear (R18(e),(f))

stand_on_stages.action: may manoeuvre alone once the give-way vessel is clearly not acting
must act to best aid avoidance; no turn to port for a vessel on her port side in a crossing (R17(c))

give_way_action.timing: early (R8(a), R16): before the TCPA alarm
give_way_action.size: substantial (R8(b)): course change large enough to be apparent, avoid a series of small alterations
give_way_action.preferred: alter course, preferably to starboard; avoid crossing ahead (R15)
give_way_action.check: check effectiveness until the other vessel is past and clear (R8(d))
